Export PDF Research compiled Oct 20, 2026 Six CRAs · 14 districts The simple version What's a CRA? A Community Redevelopment Agency is like a savings jar for one neighborhood that needs fixing up. Take a snapshot. When the CRA starts, the city writes down what all the property inside its district is worth. That's the base year . Watch it grow. As buildings get fixed up and new ones go up, the area becomes worth more. The growth fills the jar. Property tax on that extra value, the tax increment , goes into the CRA's trust fund instead of the city's and county's main budgets. It can only be spent on that neighborhood, until the CRA's end date . Why it matters: every dollar in the jar is a dollar the city and county don't have for everything else. This page shows what each jar paid for. The Property Appraiser sets it each January. Subtract any homestead exemption and you get your taxable value . Each government picks a rate. The county, the school board, your city and a few special districts each set a rate in mills . One mill is $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. Add up the slices. Your bill is every rate times your taxable value. The Tax Collector sends one bill and passes each slice to the government it belongs to. Each of these governments is a taxing authority . x: Public Money · Amendment 3 Amendment 3: what changes in Bay County if it passes On November 3, 2026, Florida voters decide Amendment 3, a property tax change. It needs at least 60% "yes" to pass. This page shows what it would do to your bill and to local budgets here, using the state's own estimates. BayCounty.me takes no position on Amendment 3. Arguments on both sides are summarized below, with sources. Export PDF Research compiled Oct 20, 2026 The simple version What Amendment 3 does A much bigger discount for homeowners. Today a homestead gets about $50,000 knocked off its value for city, county and special-district taxes. Amendment 3 raises that to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 , then grows it with inflation. School taxes don't change. Homeowners still get only the first $25,000 off for school taxes, so almost everyone keeps paying those. New Floridians wait. People who weren't Florida residents on December 31, 2026 get a $50,000 discount for their first four years, then the bigger one. Slower growth for everyone else. For rentals, businesses, second homes and land, the yearly limit on how fast the taxed value can rise drops from 10% to 5% (not for school taxes). Limits on what property tax can pay for. Cities and counties could spend it only on listed things such as public safety, schools, infrastructure, natural resources, debt and pensions, and running government. It takes effect January 1, 2027. The first bills affected would be the ones mailed in November 2027. The amendment also tells the Legislature to set up a way for cities and counties to go further and exempt homesteads completely. It estimates local governments here would collect $43.7M less in FY2029, the first full year. That's money that would stay with property owners instead. Schools lose nothing, because school taxes aren't covered. Source Year by year "Share of levy" compares the FY2029 estimate with what each government levied in FY2026, so it's a rough guide. Panama City Beach has no city property tax, so its city budget isn't affected. Source The county says that after the loss its general fund would collect about $133.5M in property tax, against $141.7M already committed to public safety, constitutional officers and other legal obligations, leaving a gap of more than $8M. It lists parks, libraries, veterans services, transit and other programs as possible cuts, and franchise fees, sales tax, EMS fees, a gas tax and impact fees as possible new revenue. After a disaster declaration, FEMA's Public Assistance program reimburses cities, the county, schools and some nonprofits for debris cleanup, emergency work and rebuilding public buildings. Each job is a "project" with its own paperwork. FEMA helps households. Individual Assistance gives grants to homeowners and renters for repairs, temporary rent and other needs. HUD funds the long rebuild. Congress later sent Florida disaster block grants (CDBG-DR), which the state handed out through "Rebuild Florida" for housing, infrastructure and downtowns. Loans and insurance fill in. SBA disaster loans and flood insurance claims went straight to residents and businesses. x: Glossary Plain-English guide Government money comes with a lot of jargon. Here is every term on this site, explained simply first, with more detail after. Anywhere on the site, a word with a dotted underline can be tapped for its short explanation. Community Redevelopment Agencies Property taxes and your bill Budgets and where money comes from How we label spending on this site Contracts, land and borrowing Public records Community Redevelopment Agencies Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) A savings jar for one neighborhood that needs fixing up. When the neighborhood's property gets more valuable, the extra tax money goes into the jar, and it can only be spent in that neighborhood. Florida law lets a city or county create a CRA for an area it officially finds run-down. The city commission usually acts as the CRA's board. It follows a written redevelopment plan and has an end date. Example: Lynn Haven's CRA covers about 695 acres around Ohio and Florida Avenues. CRA district The line drawn on the map around the neighborhood a CRA covers. Money raised inside the line is spent inside the line. Some CRAs have several districts. Panama City has four: Downtown, Downtown North, St. Andrews and Millville. Tax increment (TIF) The extra property tax a neighborhood brings in because its property became worth more after the CRA started. That extra is what fills the CRA's jar. On the day a CRA starts, the total property value inside it is written down. Every year after, the city and the county each pay into the CRA's trust fund the taxes on any value above that starting number. TIF stands for tax increment financing. Example: If a district was worth $100 million when it started and is worth $150 million now, the taxes on the $50 million difference go to the CRA. Base year The starting snapshot of how much all the property in a CRA was worth. Only growth above this number pays into the CRA. The base year is set when the CRA is created and stays the same for the life of the CRA. CRA trust fund The CRA's own bank account. Tax increment goes in, and by law it can only be spent on that CRA's plan. State law (Chapter 163, Part III) requires each CRA to keep its money in a separate trust fund and report how it was spent every year. Sunset date The day a CRA is scheduled to end. After that, the extra tax money goes back to the city and county budgets. A city can vote to extend a CRA's life. Lynn Haven extended its CRA to 2043 in January 2026. TIF rebate A deal where the CRA gives a builder back part of the new taxes their project creates, for a set number of years, to help get the project built. The rebate is paid only after the owner pays the full tax bill, and it has a maximum amount. Example: Panama City approved five TIF rebate awards downtown in December 2024. Façade or storefront grant Money a CRA gives a business owner to fix up the front of their building, usually matching what the owner spends. Most programs are 50/50: the CRA pays half, up to a limit, after the work is done. Property taxes and your bill Property tax (ad valorem tax) A tax based on what your house or land is worth. More valuable property pays more. Ad valorem is Latin for 'according to value.' Several governments each charge their own property tax, and all of them show up on one bill from the Tax Collector. Taxing authority Any government allowed to put a property tax on your bill, like the county, the school board or your city. Each one sets its own rate every year at a public hearing. Millage (mills) How property tax rates are written. One mill means $1 of tax for every $1,000 your property is taxed on. A rate of 5.5 mills is the same as 0.55%. Your bill adds up the mills from every taxing authority that covers your address. Example: 5 mills on a home taxed at $200,000 is $1,000 a year. Just value The Property Appraiser's estimate of what your property would sell for. It is set as of January 1 each year. Assessed value Your property's value after any limits on how fast it can go up. For a homestead, it usually rises more slowly than the market. Florida's Save Our Homes rule keeps a homestead's assessed value from rising more than 3% a year, or the rate of inflation if lower. Taxable value The number your tax is actually figured on: the assessed value minus any exemptions. It can be different for school taxes and other taxes, because one homestead exemption does not apply to school taxes. Homestead exemption A discount on property taxes for the home you live in full time, as long as you apply for it. The first $25,000 of value is exempt from all property taxes. A second amount, on assessed value above $50,000, is exempt from every tax except school taxes. It was $25,000 until 2024 and now rises with inflation: $25,722 in 2025 and $26,411 in 2026. Example: In 2025, a homestead assessed at $200,000 was taxed on $149,278 by the city and county and on $175,000 by the school board. Rolled-back rate The tax rate that would bring in the same money as last year from the same properties. If a government picks a higher rate, the law calls it a tax increase, even if the rate didn't change. New construction is left out of the calculation, so growth alone does not count as an increase. TRIM notice The postcard you get each August showing your proposed taxes and when the public hearings are. TRIM stands for Truth in Millage, Florida's law that sets the steps governments must follow before raising property taxes. Non-ad valorem assessment A flat fee on your tax bill for a service, like garbage pickup or fire protection. It isn't based on what your property is worth. It appears on the same bill as property taxes but is calculated per home, per acre or per unit instead of by value. MSTU An extra county tax area that pays for services in only part of the county, usually the areas outside cities. MSTU stands for Municipal Service Taxing Unit. Required Local Effort The school tax rate the state tells every school district to charge so it can get its share of state school money. The Legislature sets it each year. School boards can add a small discretionary rate and a capital rate for buildings. Save Our Homes cap A limit on how fast a homestead's taxed value can go up: 3% a year, or less if inflation is lower. Rentals, businesses and second homes have a looser 10% limit. The limits apply to assessed value, not to tax rates. Amendment 3 would lower the 10% limit to 5% for non-school taxes. Levy The total property tax a government collects in a year: its rate times all the taxable value in its area. Budgets and where money comes from Revenue Estimating Conference The state's team of economists that estimates how much money a new law or amendment would add or take away. Staff from the Legislature, the Governor's office and the Office of Economic and Demographic Research agree on one official estimate. Example: For Amendment 3, it estimated the loss for every county, city and special district. Fiscal year (FY) A government's budget year. In Florida it runs from October 1 to September 30. It is named for the year it ends in. Example: FY2026 runs from October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026. General fund A government's main checking account for everyday services like police, parks and running city hall. Most property tax goes here. Money for special purposes is kept in separate funds. Enterprise fund An account for a service you pay for directly, like water and sewer. The bills you pay cover the service. These run like a small business inside the government. Special revenue fund Money that by law can only be spent on one thing, like gas tax for roads or a CRA's trust fund. State shared revenue Money the state collects, mostly from sales tax, and sends back to cities and counties. The biggest piece is the half-cent sales tax program. Cities and counties also get revenue-sharing money based on population and other factors. Charges for services Money a government earns by charging for things it provides, like water bills, garbage pickup, permits and park fees. Intergovernmental revenue Money one government gets from another, like federal grants or state shared revenue. Constitutional officers The elected county officials named in Florida's constitution: the sheriff, property appraiser, tax collector, clerk of court and supervisor of elections. Each has its own budget, and the county pays for most of them. Audit / annual financial report A yearly check of a government's books by outside accountants, to make sure the numbers add up and the rules were followed. Florida governments must file their audits and financial reports with the state. This site uses those filings. How we label spending on this site Spent The record says the money was actually paid out. Committed A contract or award has been approved, but not all of the money has been paid yet. Budgeted Money set aside in a plan. It may or may not be spent. Proposed An idea or request that hasn't been approved. Left out of totals Shown on the site, but not added into the totals, so the same dollar is never counted twice. Examples: a change order that is already part of a project total, a possible duplicate, or money that isn't from the CRA. Contracts, land and borrowing Change order An approved change to a contract after it is signed, which often adds cost or time. Right-of-way The land a road sits on plus the strip alongside it for sidewalks, utilities and drainage. Widening a road often means buying more right-of-way. Eminent domain When a government buys private land for a public project even if the owner doesn't want to sell. A court decides the fair price. The court process is called condemnation. Bond A way for a government to borrow money now and pay it back with interest over many years, like a mortgage. The yearly payments are called debt service. Community Development District (CDD) A special government created for one development to build and pay for its roads, pipes and other basics. The property owners there pay for it. Interlocal agreement A contract between two governments, like a city and the county. Public records Public records request Asking a government to show you or send you its records. In Florida, anyone can ask, and you don't have to say why. Florida's public records law is Chapter 119 of the Florida Statutes. Governments can charge for copies and for large amounts of staff time. Check register A government's list of every payment it made: who got paid, how much, when and for what. It is the most direct way to see where money went, and most cities don't post it online.

x: About About BayCounty.me BayCounty.me is an independent project that collects Bay County, Florida public records and turns them into maps and tables anyone can read. It starts with how local governments spend public money and will grow from there. Where the information comes from Everything on the site comes from documents the public can already request or download: city and county budgets, annual reports, audits filed with the Florida Auditor General, council and commission resolutions, Bay County GIS map layers, and reporting by local newsrooms. Each figure carries a link to its source. What the labels mean Spent : the record reports the money as paid. Committed : a contract or award has been approved but is not fully paid. Budgeted or Proposed : a plan or appropriation, not a payment. Totals count each dollar once. When one record is part of another (a change order inside a project total, for example), it stays visible but is left out of the totals. Corrections If you find an error, or have a public record that fills a gap, email hello@fluxlabs.net with a link or a copy of the document. Corrections are dated on the page they affect. Who runs it BayCounty.me is built and hosted by Flux Labs , a managed IT services company in Panama City.

t: Bay County: Lack of Documented Review of Required Quarterly Reports (federal, AL 97.036 FEMA Public Assistance)
s: 3 of 40 quarterly FEMA (Hurricane Michael) reports prepared by the county's consultant did not match approved expenses and support. There was no documented county review before the consultant submitted them. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Bay County: Ineligible Expenses Approved for Reimbursement (federal, AL 97.083 SAFER fire staffing grant)
s: Two of three reimbursement requests tested included ineligible payroll costs approved by the grant administrator. The federal grantor caught them and paid only eligible costs. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Bay County: Material audit adjustments (Bay County financial statements)
s: Material adjustments were needed for the financial statements to meet GAAP because county controls did not catch them in time. Material weakness.

t: Bay County: Material adjustments - Bay County Property Appraiser
s: The Property Appraiser's office needed material adjustments to cash and accounts payable, and a check was improperly dated in its records. Material weakness.

t: Bay County: Permit fees not charged per adopted fee schedule (first reported 2020)
s: Because of problems in the permit system, the county charged some permit fees that did not match the fee schedule set by Resolutions 3945 and 3957, overcharging in some cases; the county booked a payable for the estimated excess. Auditor recommended fixing the system and remedying affected permits.

t: Bay County: Material adjustments - Bay County Sheriff
s: The Sheriff's office needed material adjustments to cash, expenses, unearned revenue, payables and accrued liabilities. Material weakness.

t: Bay County: Permit fees not charged per adopted fee schedule (Resolution 3847)
s: Permit system errors caused some permits to be charged above the adopted fee schedule.

t: Bay County: Inadequate review of component unit financial information
s: The county did not adequately review figures from a discretely presented component unit, so adjustments were needed. Significant deficiency.

t: Bay County: Material adjustments - Bay County Sheriff (repeat of 2021-001)
s: Sheriff's office needed material audit adjustments.

t: Bay District Schools: Audit Adjusting Entries (first reported 2024)
s: Significant corrections were needed, including unearned state funds not identified, an unrecorded IT subscription agreement, misclassified capital spending, and OPEB, accrual and lease adjustments. The auditor ties it partly to a lack of appropriate staffing.

t: Bay District Schools: Expenditures not limited to budgeted amounts (first reported by Auditor General as AM 2023-001)
s: General Fund spending exceeded the budget in three functional categories by a total of $326,700, and the Board did not amend the budget by September 10 as state law and Board policy require. Caused by year-end adjustments not reflected in budget monitoring.

t: Bay District Schools: Return of Title IV funds worksheets not documented as independently reviewed (federal, Pell Grant, Haney Technical College)
s: Refunds of federal student aid were calculated correctly, but there was no sign-off showing an independent review. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Bay District Schools: Return of Title IV funds not made within required timeline (federal, Pell Grant)
s: For 2 of 9 students tested, federal aid was returned to the U.S. Department of Education after the 45-day deadline because of manual-control human error. Could risk future Pell funding. Significant deficiency.

t: Bay District Schools: Multi-factor authentication not required for student information (federal, Pell / Gramm-Leach-Bliley)
s: The district's system did not require multi-factor authentication to access student information, as federal student-information security rules require. Material weakness.

t: Bay District Schools: Lack of Appropriate Staffing Leading to Audit Entries
s: Staffing shortfalls meant the district's own processes missed entries the auditors had to make. Material weakness.

t: Bay District Schools: Wage rate (Davis-Bacon) compliance (federal, COVID-19 Education Stabilization Fund AL 84.425)
s: Two construction contracts shifted mid-stream to federal pandemic funds lacked the required Davis-Bacon wage clause, and certified payrolls were not collected. Questioned costs: $773,629. Significant deficiency.

t: Bay District Schools: Expenditures not limited to budgeted amounts (repeat of AM 2023-001)
s: General Fund spending again exceeded budgeted function amounts without a timely Board amendment.
General Fund spending exceeded budgeted amounts in six functional categories by $9,532 to $218,198 (total $582,437) and the Board did not amend the budget by September 10.

t: Panama City: CRA policies, procedures and plan documents (previously 2022-002, 2023-001)
s: The city's Community Redevelopment Agency's policies, procedures and plan documents did not ensure expenditures were proper; assets could be misused or unallowable spending could occur. Reported as a material weakness.

t: Panama City: CRA policies, procedures and plan documents (previously 2022-002)
s: Same CRA policy deficiency as above.
Asset tags were missing on several capital assets and some assets could not be found for testing; procedures did not ensure assets were tagged or properly disposed of.
Bank accounts were not reconciled on a timely, regular basis, risking misappropriation or misstated records.

t: Panama City: CRA policies, procedures and plan documents
s: CRA policies did not ensure expenditures were proper.

t: Panama City: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards and State Financial Assistance (previously 2021-008)
s: Inadequate procedures to prepare the federal/state grant spending schedule, so misstatements might not be caught.
Inadequate capital asset policies (tagging, disposals).

t: Panama City: Late federal data collection form (previously 2021-011)
s: The Single Audit data collection form was not submitted on time; agencies could withhold, suspend or terminate awards.
Related timeliness finding on required report submission (same corrective action as 2022-005).

t: Panama City Beach: Lack of Documented Review of Annual Project and Expenditure Report (federal, AL 21.027 COVID-19 State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds)
s: The annual ARPA project and expenditure report to the U.S. Treasury was prepared by the grant administrator with no documented second-person review. Material weakness in internal control over compliance; no questioned costs.

t: Panama City Beach: Lack of Documented Review of Quarterly Reports (state, CSFA 43.009 Local Government Fire Services Grants)
s: None of the quarterly state fire-grant reports tested showed a documented review before submission. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Lynn Haven: Reconciliation of Account Balances, Audit Adjustments
s: Auditors had to correct journal entries to finish year-end balances, especially grant revenues and receivables, which also changed the federal/state awards schedule. Auditor cites turnover of key staff and late Hurricane Michael grant reimbursements, but noted significant improvement over the prior year.

t: Lynn Haven: Reconciliation of Account Balances and Audit Adjustments
s: Same issue; classified as a material weakness in FY2024.

t: Lynn Haven: Reconciliation of Account Balances and Audit Adjustments
s: Same issue; repeat of 2022-001; corrective action not taken.
The auditors had to make significant corrections to the city's books.

t: Springfield: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation (first reported 2007)
s: The city cannot prepare its own federal grant spending schedule; the auditors help, and multiple year-end grant entries were needed.
The pooled cash account in the ledger did not match the monthly and year-end bank reconciliations. Errors or fraud could go undetected.

t: Springfield: Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers (first reported 2015)
s: Receivables, customer deposits and payables did not agree with their detail ledgers and were not reconciled during the year.
The month-end checklist leaves out major balances, so monthly financial reports given to the Commission are not reliable.
Many revenues and expenses were posted to the wrong accounts or netted together, hiding what was really collected and spent.
Small staff means one person can approve, record and have custody of assets, including broad accounting system access.

t: Springfield: Actual Expenditures Exceeded Budget in the General Fund
s: General Fund spending exceeded the final adopted budget by about $8,069,872 without a budget amendment, violating s. 166.241(3) F.S. The auditor suggested budgeting for debt proceeds and similar sources (the year included the $15 million city complex loan).
Significant auditor corrections required.

t: Springfield: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation
s: City cannot prepare its federal awards schedule.
Cash in the ledger did not match bank reconciliations.

t: Springfield: Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers
s: Receivables, deposits and payables not reconciled to detail ledgers.
Incomplete month-end close.
Revenues and expenses misclassified or netted.
Incompatible duties not separated.

t: Springfield: Collection and Write-off Policies and Procedures (first reported 2020)
s: No written policy for sending unpaid accounts to collections or writing them off, so receivables may be overstated and customers treated inconsistently.

t: Springfield: Final Budget Not Approved Within the Allowed Time Period
s: The FY2024 budget was amended in February 2025, after the deadline in state law.

t: Springfield: Timely Reporting Requirements for Grants
s: Single Audit package not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse because of staffing shortages and the many corrections needed.

t: Springfield: Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund - City Allocation
s: Over three years the city did not calculate and pay its share of tax increment to its own CRA, underfunding the CRA trust fund by an estimated $291,027 (material weakness).
Significant auditor corrections required.

t: Springfield: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation
s: City cannot prepare its federal awards schedule.
Cash not reconciled to bank.

t: Springfield: Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers
s: Detail ledgers not reconciled.
Incomplete month-end close.
Incompatible duties not separated.

t: Springfield: Collection and Write-off Policies and Procedures
s: No written collections/write-off policy.
The auditors had to propose adjustments before the city's books met accounting standards (GAAP). Material weakness. First reported in 2007.

t: Parker: Lack of Segregation of Duties (first reported 2009)
s: Too few staff to separate incompatible duties; material weakness reported since 2009.

t: Parker: Reporting Requirements for Grants (first reported 2023)
s: The audit was not finished within 9 months of year end, so the federal Single Audit package was not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. The city could lose grant funding.

t: Parker: Insufficient Documentation Supporting Law Enforcement Trust Fund Revenue
s: The city booked $36,652 from disposed criminal-case evidence as Law Enforcement Trust Fund revenue but could not show a forfeiture judgment or court order proving the money legally belonged to the city. Revenue and fund balance may be overstated by $36,652.

t: Parker: Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund (first reported 2024)
s: State law (s. 163.387 F.S.) requires each taxing authority to pay its tax increment to the CRA by January 1. The county paid 4 days late and the city did not pay its own share before year end, leaving the CRA trust fund short about $122,929.
Employee data sent to the actuary for the retiree-health (OPEB) valuation had multiple errors, producing an inaccurate valuation and delaying the audit.

t: Parker: Retirement Expense Not Reviewed Timely and Rates Not Updated
s: The city did not update new state FRS contribution rates effective July 1, 2025 in its payroll system for months, understating retirement expense and liability by about $20,000.
Auditor-proposed adjustments needed to meet GAAP.

t: Parker: Lack of Segregation of Duties
s: Too few staff to separate duties.

t: Parker: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards
s: Weak controls over preparing the financial statements and the federal awards schedule (material weakness); repeat of 2023-003 and 2022-003.

t: Parker: Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund - City Allocation
